nodes.title: Economic conditions and macroeconomic policy transmission
nodes.recommended_depth: A-level / UK Level 3 Business, not an Economics course

teaching_content.core_explanation: Businesses operate within an economy whose growth, inflation, interest rates, labour-market conditions, taxation and public spending affect demand, costs, finance and confidence. Economic growth refers to an increase in real economic output, but its effect on a particular business depends on industry and customer income sensitivity. Inflation is sustained increase in the general price level; individual prices can rise or fall differently. Interest rates influence the cost of borrowing, returns to saving and spending/investment decisions, but effects differ according to debt levels, customer sensitivity and contract structures. Labour-market conditions affect wage pressure, recruitment difficulty and consumer incomes. Government fiscal policy changes taxation and public expenditure; monetary policy influences interest rates and financial conditions. A Business learner does not need a full macroeconomic model, but should be able to trace transmission: policy or economic change -> household/business behaviour -> demand/cost/finance -> firm-specific consequences. Policies can create mixed effects. Higher interest rates may weaken discretionary demand and raise debt cost while increasing interest income for cash-rich firms; higher public investment may raise demand in some sectors while contributing to tax/borrowing trade-offs elsewhere.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Economic analysis is only useful when learners connect macro conditions to the particular business rather than memorising 'inflation bad' or 'growth good'.
definitions: economic growth: increase in real economic output over time
inflation: sustained increase in general price level
interest rate: price of borrowing/return on lending or saving
unemployment: people without work who are available/seeking under the relevant measure
fiscal policy: government decisions on taxation and public spending
monetary policy: policy affecting interest rates/financial conditions to pursue macro objectives
important_boundaries: inflation is not every price rising equally
economic growth does not increase every firm's sales
higher rates are not universally bad
business analysis of policy should focus on transmission rather than political judgement
nominal growth can differ from real growth
facts: interest-rate changes affect borrowers/savers differently
inflation can affect both input costs and selling prices
tight labour markets can raise recruitment difficulty and wage pressure
tax/spending changes alter disposable income and sector demand
mechanisms: higher rate -> borrowing cost and saving incentive -> consumption/investment change -> firm demand
inflation -> input/wage cost + customer purchasing power -> margin/demand
fiscal change -> disposable income/public procurement -> demand
labour shortage -> wage pressure/recruitment delay -> capacity/service
causal_relationships: macro condition/policy -> exposure channel -> firm-specific cost/demand/cash -> strategic response
interest rate -> finance cost -> gearing risk -> investment
examples: A heavily indebted housebuilder can be hit by higher finance costs and weaker mortgage affordability, while a bank or cash-rich company has a different exposure.
non_examples: Writing 'inflation increases costs so profit falls' without considering pricing power, wage timing, product mix or customer demand.
real_world_transfer: Explain why the same interest-rate rise can harm one company and benefit another.
Distinguish nominal sales growth caused partly by inflation from stronger real demand.
assumptions: Other influences are separated sufficiently for the mechanism to be useful.
limitations: Policy effects operate with lags and interact; forecasts are uncertain; businesses respond adaptively.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Higher interest rates are bad for all businesses.
misconceptions.correction: Effects depend on borrowing, cash holdings, customer finance sensitivity, sector and pricing response.

interpretation: economic indicators are context, not deterministic forecasts
common_errors: assuming direction of effect without transmission mechanism

uncertainties: Exact macro policy depth varies by qualification.

nodes.title: Competition, market power, consumer protection and regulation

teaching_content.core_explanation: Competition is the process by which businesses and alternatives contest customers, resources or economic value. It can pressure firms to improve price, quality, efficiency and innovation, though outcomes vary by market. Market power is the ability to act with reduced competitive constraint—for example by raising price or worsening terms without losing enough business to make the action unprofitable. Market share can be evidence of power but does not prove it: the relevant market definition, substitute products, barriers to entry, buyer power and switching costs matter. Regulation sets rules or constraints intended to address market failures, safety, information asymmetry, fairness, competition or other public objectives. Consumer protection regulates how businesses market, price and sell, including transparency and misleading claims. Regulation can create compliance costs and constrain tactics, but can also create trust, minimum standards and a more functional market. Strong business analysis therefore asks what behaviour the rule changes, how compliance affects cost/capability, and whether the regulation changes competition or customer trust.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Competition and regulation shape pricing, entry, strategy and customer relationships and require learners to avoid simplistic 'regulation is a cost' reasoning.
definitions: competition: rivalry/alternative choice affecting business behaviour
market power: ability to operate with reduced competitive constraint
barrier to entry: obstacle increasing difficulty/cost of market entry
regulation: rules imposed by public/legal authority
consumer protection: rules protecting customers from specified unfair/misleading/unsafe practices
important_boundaries: market share is not market power
competitor count is not enough to measure competition
regulation can create benefits as well as costs
legal compliance is not the same as ethical excellence
facts: switching costs and substitutes affect market power
entry barriers can protect incumbents
regulatory standards can alter cost and entry conditions
mechanisms: more effective alternatives -> price/quality pressure
entry barrier -> reduced new-entry threat -> incumbent power
consumer rule -> disclosure/process change -> cost and trust effects
causal_relationships: market structure -> competitive pressure -> price/quality/innovation -> profitability/customer outcome
examples: A firm with 60% share can still face significant constraint if customers can switch to a different technology easily; conversely a smaller supplier of a unique critical input may possess strong bargaining power.
non_examples: Calling a business a monopoly simply because it is the largest firm.
real_world_transfer: Question a pricing strategy that ignores transparency and consumer-protection requirements.
assumptions: Relevant market/substitute boundaries can be defined meaningfully.
limitations: Market power is dynamic and multi-dimensional; regulation differs by sector and changes over time.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Regulation is bad for business because it raises costs.
misconceptions.correction: Regulation can raise compliance costs but can also increase trust, reduce harmful competition and set common standards.

methods: market-share measures support but do not determine power analysis
interpretation: quantitative concentration indicators require market-definition context

models_frameworks: Five Forces can support structural analysis through BUS-STR-005

nodes.title: Globalisation, international trade, market entry, FDI and protectionism

teaching_content.core_explanation: International business occurs when firms sell, source, invest or coordinate activities across national borders. Globalisation describes increasing cross-border integration of markets, production, finance, information and business networks; it is uneven across sectors and can strengthen or retreat over time. Firms internationalise to access customers, resources, skills, lower costs, diversification or strategic assets, but cross-border activity adds currency, logistics, legal, cultural, political and coordination complexity. Exporting sells output from one country into another. Licensing allows another party to use specified intellectual property or business rights. Franchising grants a business format/brand under contract. Joint ventures share ownership/control of an activity, while foreign direct investment (FDI) involves acquiring or establishing lasting business operations in another country. Direct investment offers greater control but normally requires more capital and exposure. Trade policy changes the economics of international business. Tariffs tax imports; quotas limit quantities; subsidies support specified domestic activity; trading blocs or trade agreements can reduce barriers among members. Protectionism can protect selected domestic producers in the short run but can raise input/customer costs, provoke retaliation or reduce competitive pressure. The business effect depends on whether the firm imports, exports, competes with imports, uses foreign inputs or invests abroad.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: The board challenge showed that the original globalisation node was too broad. This expanded node now contains the actual mechanisms needed to map major A-level international-business requirements.
definitions: globalisation: increased cross-border integration of economic/business activity
exporting: selling domestically produced goods/services into foreign markets
licensing: contractual permission to use specified IP/rights
franchising: contractual replication of a business format/brand
joint venture: jointly owned/controlled activity
FDI: lasting investment/control in business operations in another country
tariff: tax on imports
quota: quantitative restriction on imports
subsidy: financial support lowering cost/supporting activity
trading bloc: group of economies with reduced internal trade barriers under specified rules
protectionism: policies restricting foreign competition or supporting domestic producers
important_boundaries: globalisation is not simply exporting
FDI is not the same as portfolio investment or exporting
offshoring is not necessarily outsourcing
protectionism can create winners and losers within the same country
lower foreign wage rates do not equal lower total cost
facts: entry mode trades control against capital/risk
international expansion can diversify revenue but add complexity
trade barriers can affect both final goods and imported inputs
mechanisms: export/entry -> larger market -> revenue potential + localisation/logistics risk
FDI -> local control/capability -> capital/geopolitical exposure
tariff on imported input -> higher cost -> price/margin/sourcing response
tariff on competing imports -> weaker foreign price competition -> possible domestic benefit but lower pressure/retaliation risk
causal_relationships: trade policy -> import/export economics -> cost/demand -> strategic response
global sourcing -> lead time/currency/geopolitical exposure -> inventory/resilience
examples: A UK food brand can enter a foreign market through exporting, licensing a local producer, franchising retail operations, a joint venture or owned FDI; each changes control, investment and risk.
An import tariff can help a domestic producer competing with imports while simultaneously raising costs for another domestic firm that uses the taxed input.
non_examples: Saying protectionism 'helps domestic business' without identifying which businesses buy or sell the affected goods.
Calling a distributor agreement FDI when no lasting ownership/investment exists.
real_world_transfer: Explain why a business may choose licensing over FDI despite earning less per sale.
Identify a domestic business harmed by a policy intended to protect another domestic industry.
assumptions: Political/legal/trade rules are current and verified; cultural differences are evidenced rather than stereotyped.
limitations: International rules are complex and change; broad labels such as 'emerging market' can conceal major country differences.

misconceptions.correction: International activity can lower some costs but adds logistics, inventory, coordination, currency, compliance and disruption exposure.
Effects depend on whether firms compete with, use or sell into the protected trade flows.

methods: market growth/share, currency conversion and tariff-cost scenarios where relevant
worked_examples: A 10% tariff on an imported component costing £100 before tariff adds £10 direct tariff cost before logistics/tax interactions; business effect depends on ability to switch supplier or pass on cost.
common_errors: assuming tariff effect only hits foreign seller

models_frameworks: course-specific international strategy frameworks should remain separate from factual mechanisms
uncertainties: Exact named trading blocs, current tariffs and legal procedures are time-sensitive/course-specific.

teaching_content.core_explanation: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in another. Appreciation means a currency becomes more valuable relative to another currency; depreciation means it becomes less valuable. For a UK business, a stronger pound generally makes foreign-currency imports cheaper in pounds and UK-produced exports more expensive to foreign buyers if foreign-currency prices adjust fully. A weaker pound tends to reverse those effects. Real business consequences are more complicated because firms may both import and export, price in different currencies, hedge currency exposure, use contracts fixed in advance or face competitors whose costs also move. Exchange-rate changes therefore affect input costs, selling prices, demand, cash flow and competitiveness through specific exposure channels. A weaker pound can support an exporter with mainly UK costs but harm an exporter heavily dependent on imported components. Competitiveness also depends on productivity, quality, brand and service—not just currency.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Exchange-rate reasoning is a strong test of conditional analysis: memorised 'weak pound helps exporters' statements are incomplete without the firm's cost and pricing structure.
definitions: exchange rate: price of one currency in another
appreciation: rise in currency value relative to another
depreciation: fall in currency value
hedging: action intended to reduce exposure to adverse currency movement
competitiveness: ability to win business relative to alternatives based on price and non-price factors
important_boundaries: weak currency is not always good for exporters
exchange rate movement is not the only source of international competitiveness
quoted rate direction matters
hedging reduces specified exposure but has cost/limits
facts: currency movement changes translated import/export prices
contract timing can delay effects
mixed import/export exposure can offset or amplify effects
mechanisms: appreciation -> cheaper imports -> lower input cost
appreciation -> higher foreign-currency price for unchanged sterling export price -> possible weaker demand
hedge -> greater cash certainty -> opportunity/cost trade-off
causal_relationships: currency -> import cost/export price -> margin/demand -> cash/strategy
examples: Sterling strengthens from £1=$1.25 to £1=$1.35. A $135 component falls from £108 to £100 before other effects, benefiting a UK importer.
non_examples: Saying a weaker pound is always good for UK business.
real_world_transfer: Explain why two UK exporters can react differently to the same sterling depreciation.
assumptions: Quoted rate is interpreted correctly and other prices/contracts are held sufficiently constant for the first-order effect.
limitations: Pass-through can be incomplete; competitors, inflation, contracts and hedging change final effects.

misconceptions.correction: It can improve foreign price competitiveness, but imported input costs, hedging, pricing and demand elasticity can offset or reverse the benefit.

methods.name: Currency conversion
methods.formula: apply the quoted exchange relationship consistently
methods.interpretation: The dollar cost translates to £100 at that rate.

interpretation: State quote direction and business exposure.

nodes.title: Ethics, corporate responsibility and accountability

teaching_content.core_explanation: Business ethics concerns what actions and decisions are justified, fair or responsible, not merely what is legal or profitable. Corporate responsibility concerns how a business recognises and manages consequences for customers, employees, suppliers, communities, owners and the environment. Compliance establishes minimum obligations; ethical judgement can go beyond those minima. Ethical behaviour can support trust, retention and reputation, but it should not be reduced to a marketing tactic because some responsible choices create real costs or constrain profitable opportunities. Accountability means decision makers can be required to explain actions and face consequences; governance, reporting, stakeholder voice and regulation can support it. Ethical conflicts are often genuine trade-offs rather than simple good-versus-bad choices—for example, a business may need to balance affordability for customers, fair supplier terms, employee pay and investment in safer production. Strong evaluation identifies affected stakeholders, rights/obligations, magnitude, uncertainty and alternatives rather than asserting that 'ethical businesses make more profit'.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Ethics prevents the subject from treating profit as the only criterion and links governance, stakeholder trade-offs, supply chains and sustainability.
definitions: business ethics: reasoning about justified/right conduct in business decisions
corporate responsibility: organisational responsibility for wider social/environmental/stakeholder consequences
accountability: obligation to explain and answer for decisions
compliance: meeting applicable legal/regulatory requirements
important_boundaries: legal is not automatically ethical
ethical is not automatically profitable
CSR is not philanthropy alone
reputation benefit does not prove ethical motive or outcome
facts: businesses can create external effects beyond contracted parties
ethical expectations vary but legal and professional standards constrain conduct
responsible supply-chain choices can change costs and risk
mechanisms: ethical conduct -> trust/relationship -> possible retention/reputation
unethical conduct -> harm -> legal/reputational/employee/customer consequences
governance/reporting -> accountability -> behaviour incentives
causal_relationships: decision -> stakeholder harm/benefit -> response/regulation/trust -> business outcome
examples: A company can legally pressure a small supplier with severe payment terms yet still face ethical questions about dependency and downstream harm.
non_examples: Calling charitable donations proof of responsible core operations while ignoring harmful labour or environmental practices.
real_world_transfer: Question whether a 'responsible business' claim concerns core operations or peripheral philanthropy.
assumptions: Claims are evaluated against evidence of actual conduct and impacts.
limitations: Ethical values can conflict; consequences are uncertain; stakeholder impacts can be difficult to compare.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Ethical behaviour is good business because customers reward it.
misconceptions.correction: Ethical choices may create commercial benefits, but ethical justification does not depend on profitability and some choices impose real costs.

interpretation: ethical impacts can include quantitative evidence but cannot always be reduced to money

models_frameworks: course-specific CSR frameworks such as Carroll should remain model entries, not factual truth

nodes.title: Sustainability, net zero, environmental claims and ESG reporting

teaching_content.core_explanation: Business sustainability concerns whether economic activity can continue while managing environmental and social impacts over time. Environmental analysis includes energy, greenhouse-gas emissions, material use, water, waste, pollution and supply-chain effects. Net zero is not the same as producing no emissions anywhere; it involves deep reduction of greenhouse-gas emissions and balancing residual emissions within a defined boundary using credible removals or other accepted mechanisms. Environmental claims must be specific, evidence-based and clear about scope; a recyclable package does not prove the whole product has low environmental impact. ESG (environmental, social and governance) reporting organises selected non-financial information about impacts, risks and governance. Reporting is not the same as performance: a business can disclose extensively while still producing poor outcomes, and metrics can be chosen or framed selectively. Sustainability decisions can reduce energy/material costs or risk, open markets and support trust, but often require investment and can create trade-offs. Lifecycle thinking is important because shifting emissions or harm upstream does not necessarily improve the whole system.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Sustainability is both a genuine business constraint/opportunity and a high-risk area for vague claims; learners need mechanisms, boundaries and evidence literacy.
definitions: sustainability: managing activity so economic, environmental and social systems remain viable over time
net zero: deep emissions reduction plus balancing residual emissions within a defined boundary
greenwashing: misleading/exaggerated environmental representation
ESG: environmental, social and governance dimensions used in reporting/analysis
lifecycle: stages from inputs/production through use and end-of-life
important_boundaries: ESG reporting is not ESG performance
net zero is not zero emissions
recyclable is not proof of lower total environmental impact
carbon reduction in one stage can be offset elsewhere
facts: supply chains can contain material environmental/social impacts
environmental improvements can reduce cost or require investment
claims require evidence and scope
mechanisms: energy/process change -> emissions/cost -> investment/payback
traceability -> better impact data -> improved control/claim credibility
misleading claim -> consumer/regulatory/reputation risk
causal_relationships: operations/sourcing -> environmental impact -> regulation/customer/investor response -> strategy/finance
measurement/reporting -> transparency -> decision/accountability, but not automatic improvement
examples: Switching to lighter packaging may lower material and transport emissions, but a lifecycle assessment should also consider recyclability, product protection and waste if damage rises.
non_examples: Calling a product 'green' because one component is recycled without defining the overall comparison.
real_world_transfer: Question an ESG report that lists metrics without targets, boundaries or evidence of outcomes.
assumptions: Impact boundaries and measurement methods are clear enough for comparison.
limitations: Environmental/social metrics can be incomplete and non-comparable; future regulation/technology changes rapidly.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: ESG reporting proves a business is sustainable.
misconceptions.correction: Reporting describes selected information; actual performance and impact must be assessed separately.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Net zero means a company produces no emissions.
misconceptions.correction: It requires deep reduction and balancing of residual emissions within a defined boundary.

methods: percentage emission/resource change and investment appraisal where data permit
interpretation: quantitative environmental claims require stated scope/baseline

models_frameworks: Triple Bottom Line may be a course-specific analytical framework
uncertainties: Detailed ESG reporting standards are evolving and should not be frozen as timeless subject truth.

nodes.title: Risk, contingency planning and crisis resilience

teaching_content.core_explanation: Risk management identifies uncertainties that can affect objectives, considers their likelihood and consequences, and chooses responses such as avoidance, reduction, transfer, acceptance or preparation. Contingency planning specifies actions, responsibilities, resources and communication for plausible disruptions. Crisis management deals with events that threaten important operations, stakeholders or reputation and often require rapid decisions with incomplete information. Resilience is broader: the capacity to absorb shocks, adapt and recover while maintaining critical functions. Insurance transfers specified financial consequences but cannot transfer all customer, operational or reputational effects. Diversification, redundant suppliers, data backups, financial buffers, spare capacity and rehearsed plans all have costs in normal periods but can preserve option value during disruption. Good risk analysis avoids false precision: a low-probability event with catastrophic consequences can justify action, while probability estimates themselves may be weak.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Risk and resilience integrate finance, supply chain, operations, people and strategy and teach decisions under uncertainty rather than after-the-fact explanations.
definitions: risk management: process of identifying/assessing/responding to uncertainty affecting objectives
contingency plan: prepared response for specified disruption
crisis: severe event requiring urgent coordinated response
resilience: ability to absorb, adapt and recover
risk transfer: shifting specified financial/contractual consequences to another party
important_boundaries: insurance does not remove operational/reputation risk
contingency is not prediction
resilience is not maximum redundancy
low probability does not mean unimportant
facts: critical dependencies create concentration risk
plans need testing and updating
buffers have opportunity costs
mechanisms: diversification -> lower single-point dependency -> resilience but complexity/cost
contingency rehearsal -> faster coordinated response -> lower disruption
financial buffer -> liquidity during shock -> survival option
causal_relationships: risk event -> operational impact -> stakeholder response -> cash/reputation -> recovery
examples: A manufacturer dual-sources a critical component at higher normal cost because single-supplier failure would stop production entirely.
non_examples: Calling an insured factory fully protected from fire risk while ignoring lost production and customers.
real_world_transfer: Explain why apparent 'unused' capacity or backup suppliers can have economic value as insurance-like options.
assumptions: Risk information is imperfect and scenarios need periodic review.
limitations: Rare events are difficult to estimate; plans can fail under novel combinations of events.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Risk management tries to eliminate risk.
misconceptions.correction: It decides which risks to avoid, reduce, transfer, accept or prepare for while recognising residual uncertainty.

methods: scenario, sensitivity and expected-value tools from BUS-EVI-003/004 can support risk decisions
interpretation: probability-weighted measures should not obscure catastrophic downside or weak probability estimates
